summary:
Project Title: Project Odyssey: Celestial Ascent & Orbital Transfer
Tagline: A physics-driven 2D space flight and resource management simulator built in Godot.
Core Concept: Inspired by classic physics-climbing mechanics (such as Hill Climb Racing), the player manages a spacecraft navigating variable gravitational fields and rough planetary surfaces. Players upgrade thrusters, fuel tanks, and attitude control systems in a Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB) to successfully complete transfers across celestial bodies like the Moon, Mars, and Europa.
details: What does it do, and how does it work? Celestial Ascent & Orbital Transfer is an interactive, physics-driven flight and resource management game inspired by classic 2D climbing mechanics (such as Hill Climb Racing) but grounded in real space exploration physics. The Garage Loop (The Hangar): Players start in a virtual hangar (Vehicle Assembly Building) where they manage limited funding. Players make crucial trade-offs by upgrading three core sub-systems: Propulsion (Specific Impulse): Increases thrust power but burns more fuel. Propellant Tanks: Expands fuel capacity to withstand longer burns. Attitude Control (RCS): Improves rotational torque for tilting and stabilizes the spacecraft's landing/position. The Physics-Based Flight: Unlike arcade shooters, players do not have direct positional control. Instead, the spaceship is a physics RigidBody2D that uses manual thrust and torque (rotation) forces in simulated low-gravity environments. Planetary Missions: Players pick a mission based on celestial bodies like the Moon, Mars, or Europa. Each features its own: Real-world scaled gravitational constants affecting thrust requirements. Custom target transfer distances to achieve success. Procedural bumpy terrains with variable slopes and obstacles. Resources & Traversal: While traversing, players must combat gravity and manage dwindling fuel while picking up scarce propellant canisters (RCS fuels) scattered across the terrain to sustain flight and eventually reach the target orbital transfer distance. What benefits does it have? Accessible Physics Education: Demonstrates complex spacecraft maneuvers—such as the balance between thrust, mass, inertia, and variable gravity wells—without the steep learning curve of simulators like Kerbal Space Program. Risk vs. Reward Decision-making: Emphasizes resource stewardship. Players must evaluate when to burn fuel to gain distance versus when to drift and rely on inertia to survive on a limited budget. Demonstration of the Rocket Equation: Educates the public on how mass (upgrades) and environments (gravity) drastically impact propulsion efficiency. What is the intended impact of the project? Public Engagement: Inspires curiosity in astrophysics and aerospace engineering by transforming daunting mission data (like specific impulse, RCS, and planetary gravity) into gamified, touch-and-feel mechanics. Educational Scalability: Acts as an interactive classroom tool for B.Tech, physics, or high school programs, proving that aerospace principles can be taught through play. NASA Open Data Awareness: Creates a direct visual and gameplay pipeline to help non-experts appreciate the mission challenges and environmental profiles of visiting the Moon, Mars, and Europa. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? Game Engine: Godot Engine 4.x, utilizing its 2D physics engine (RigidBody2D for realistic flight mechanics and StaticBody2D for planetary terrain). Programming Language: GDScript, used for UI behaviors, procedural terrain calculations, and physics integration. Design & Graphics Software: Built entirely in-engine using standard procedurally rendered polygons (Polygon2D and CollisionPolygon2D), visual shaders, and UI Controls to ensure rapid prototyping and small file sizes. Math & Algorithms: Utilized 1D noise algorithms (FastNoiseLite) to procedurally generate variable planetary hills, valleys, and obstacle matrices based on real-world target profiles. Development Hardware: Tested on general-purpose laptops (e.g., standard integrated graphics with 8GB RAM), maintaining 60 FPS by leveraging Godot’s lightweight, highly optimized Compatibility Renderer. How is your project creative? Rather than developing a traditional, straightforward 2D space shooter, our project introduces lateral gravity-to-terrain scaling. While most space games ignore gravity, we simulated it relative to surface traversal. By utilizing a "climbing" mechanic on horizontal terrain to simulate horizontal orbital transfer and planetary escaping, we gave tangible form to the invisible, gravity-dominated battle of rocketry. Additionally, we designed the entire system to be 100% procedural and asset-free. Every visual hill, every spaceship component, and every ui-state button is drawn entirely through code and geometric polygons. This keeps our project's final application footprint under a few megabytes while still offering endless dynamic gameplay. What factors did our team consider? User Experience (UX): Space sims are notoriously hard for newcomers. We considered simplicity by using a familiar 3-key control mapping (Thrust, Left/Right Rotation) with arcade styling, yet retained accurate under-the-hood gravitational mechanics. NASA Mission Veracity: Designed planetary values that correspond with actual scientific data. Spacecraft inertia feels drastically different on Europa (~0.13g) than it does on Earth-sized benchmarks, honoring realistic aerospace constraints. Software Portability: By leveraging the ultra-light Godot engine and keeping external game assets at a minimum, the simulation is easy to ship, install, and run on low-resource machines, ensuring it remains highly accessible. Modular Integration: Kept code bases separated via Global Singleton patterns, which allows future developer teams to easily integrate active NASA APIs or complex landscape terrains without breaking core physics systems.
